                        EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

       Whitis Land Investments, LP (“Whitis”) submits these Exceptions to the Proposal for

Decision in this Docket and requests that the ALJs and the Commission consider the following:

                                          I.   INTRODUCTION

       Whitis supports the ALJs’ recommendation that the Commission deny Oncor’s and LCRA’s

(collectively, “Applicants”) applications for the Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project and the Big

Hill-to-Sand Lake Project (collectively, “Import Path 2”). After thoroughly reviewing the record

evidence and applicable law, the ALJs correctly concluded that Applicants failed to prove the need

for Import Path 2 for four reasons.

       First, neither the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”) nor HB 5066 establishes a

collective need for the project, as occurred in the CREZ cases. Here, Applicants were required to

demonstrate the need for Import Path 2 “separate and apart from the from the three 765-kV import

paths as one comprehensive project,” 1 and failed to do so.



       1
           PFD at 99.

Intervenor: Whitis Land Investments, LP
Reply Brief                                                                            Page 1 of 8
        Second, Applicants failed to show that the PBRP’s projected loads established a need for

Import Path 2. Because Applicants did not provide updated load projections, much less a

substantiated load, they could not demonstrate that a need for Import Path 2 persisted despite

changed circumstances.

       Third, Applicants failed to show that sufficient generation would be available at Bell

County East to import the necessary power into the Permian Basin. Indeed, the record does not

establish whether Import Path 2 can serve concurrent loads in Central and West Texas.

       Finally, the ALJs identified credible record evidence demonstrating that new and planned

generation in the Permian Basin could meet or exceed the PBRP’s load projections. Applicants did

not adequately address this evidence and, therefore, failed to show that new and planned generation

would not meet the PBRP’s load projections.

       Each of these four reasons independently supports denying the applications. Together, the

applications’ shortcomings are insurmountable. Whitis therefore requests that the Commission

deny the applications for the Import Path 2 projects. Alternatively, if the Commission declines to

follow the ALJs’ recommendation, Whitis submits the following Exceptions to the PFD’s

alternative routing analysis.

      II.   EXCEPTIONS TO THE SELECTION OF ROUTE 894 OR ANY ROUTE CONTAINING LINK F1

       Should the Commission determine that the record satisfies the requirement for an

independent showing of need, Whitis submits these exceptions to the PFD’s recommendation of

Route 894. The record demonstrates that Route 894 is not the superior route and that Whitis Route

1-14 is the best-performing route in this docket.




Intervenor: Whitis Land Investments, LP
Reply Brief                                                                             Page 2 of 8
 A.      Whitis Route 1-14 provides savings over all Routes of Interest in the PFD.

        The PFD stated that cost was not a distinguishing factor among the focus routes. 2 Route

487 was the least expensive focus route discussed in the PFD, at $1,664,814,000. 3 Whitis Route

1-14, at $1,645,197,000, costs $19,617,000 less than Route 487 and $35,722,000 less than Route

8944. Although cost alone may not distinguish the routes for the ALJs, the other factors identified

in the PFD make these cost differences relevant.

B.      Route 894’s benefit on habitable structure count comes at a high cost.

        Although Route 894 has fewer habitable structures, Whitis Route 1-14 is superior because

Route 894’s cost per habitable structure avoided greatly exceeds Commission precedent. In PUC

Docket No. 51023, the Commission selected Route Z2 and treated habitable-structure count and

cost as distinguishing factors. Route R1 had 19 fewer habitable structures than Route Z2 but carried

a $5.88 million cost premium. The Commission noted that “[e]ach of the 19 additional structures

avoided by route R1 is avoided at an average cost of $309,000 per structure.” 5 The Commission

explained that its analysis of residential impacts should focus on the policy of prudent avoidance.

Prudent avoidance is defined as “[t]he limiting of exposures to electric and magnetic fields that

can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort.” 6 Route 894 avoids additional

structures at an unreasonable cost.

        Here, Whitis Route 1-14 satisfies the policy of prudent avoidance while eliminating a cost

per structure avoided that is more than twice the amount in Docket No. 51023. Whitis Route 1-14

has 140 habitable structures within 500 feet of the line, compared with Route 894’s 85. Viewed in

 isolation, that difference appears to give Route 894 a distinct advantage. But under the

Commission’s analysis in Docket No. 51023, Route 894’s advantage disappears. Route 894 carries

a $35,722,000 premium over Whitis Route 1-14, or $649,490.91 per habitable structure avoided. 7

The Commission and the ALJs should therefore consider Whitis Route 1-14 because Route 894’s

cost per habitable structure avoided is more than twice the average in Docket No. 51023.

C.   Whitis Route 1-14 avoids Link F1 and multiple cultural resources and
major developments.

         Whitis Route 1-14 crosses one cultural-resource site, while Routes 296, 487, and 894 each

cross two or more. Link F1 is common to all three routes and contains a cultural-resource site that

any route using Link F1 would cross.8

         In addition, Link F1 disregards apparent property lines and bisects two cohesive properties:

Whitis and Solana Ranch.9 Both properties are under development, and both parties have invested

substantial time and money in their development. Together, the developments will contain

approximately 18,000 homes.10 These homes are intended to accommodate rapid growth along the

I-35 corridor near Salado. On Whitis’s property alone, Link F1 would affect approximately 672

single-family residential lots.11 Reducing the supply of available homes will increase single-family

home prices, contrary to the community value of preserving the availability of affordable housing.

Should the Commission approve any route in the application, Whitis asks the Commission to

require Applicants to minimize property-bisection impacts, as it ordered in Docket Nos. 59315 and

59029.

 D.     Whitis Route 1-14 creates less new ROW and contains fewer unknowns.

       Whitis Route 1-14 parallels compatible rights-of-way for 107.64 miles. 12 Only Route 487

and CCG perform better among the focus routes in this docket.13 However, at 215.91 miles, Whitis

Route 1-14 is shorter than every route discussed in the PFD.14 As a percentage of total route length,

Whitis Route 1-14 parallels existing compatible rights-of-way for 49.85%, outperforming all

Focus Routes in the PFD.15

       The PFD separately considers the extent to which a route parallels existing compatible

infrastructure, including transmission lines and roadways, and expresses this measure as a

percentage of total route length. Whitis Route 1-14 parallels existing compatible infrastructure for

10.87% of its length.16 Route 894 does so for only 4.53%.17

       Whitis Route 1-14 parallels 6.34 percentage points more existing compatible infrastructure

than Route 894 and creates fewer unknowns than a route crossing previously undisturbed land. 18

Applicants acknowledged that, while building any transmission project, “the less uncertainty, the

better.”19 Whitis 1-14 is the superior route for minimizing this risk.

E.   Whitis Route 1-14’s proximity to Colorado Bend State Park is not
outcome determinative.

       Under Commission precedent and the application of prudent avoidance, Whitis Route 1-

14’s benefits outweigh Route 894’s marginal benefit regarding parks and recreational areas. In

PUC Docket No. 30168, the Commission stated that it had previously emphasized two factors

 when routing transmission lines: line cost and impacts on habitable structures. 20 It determined that

the ALJs placed too much weight on recreational and park areas, historical values, and

environmental issues.21 The Commission’s analysis contextualizes these issues. “[W]hile Route 20

is in close proximity to the LBJ National Grasslands, it does not cross, bisect, or encroach on any

actively managed tract within the Grasslands.22

        Here, both Whitis Route 1-14 and Route 487 include Link J11, which passes within 1,000

feet of Colorado Bend State Park. Link J11 does not cross, bisect, or encroach on the park.

Nevertheless, the PFD emphasized Route 487’s proximity to the park, highlighting that it is the

only Focus Route passing within 1,000 feet of a park or recreational area. Conversely, the PFD

recognized Route 894’s marginal benefit of reduced visibility from many areas of Colorado Bend

State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park.

        Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (“TPWD”) neither intervened nor filed comments in

this docket. “TPWD did not provide recommendations or informational comments to the

Commission in this docket within the meaning of the referred issue.” 23 The PFD found that the

recommendations in TPWD’s pre-filing letter were considered and “substantially addressed by the

mitigation measures Mr. Poole recommends and by Applicants’ standard practices.” 24

        Impacts on parks and recreational areas should be analyzed under the Commission’s prior

guidance. Whitis Route 1-14 does not cross, bisect, or encroach on Colorado Bend State Park.

Accordingly, Whitis requests that the Commission and ALJs give greater weight to Whitis Route

benefit concerning parks and recreational areas.

F.    Whitis Route 1-14 surpasses Route 894 on Community and Historic
Values.

       Whitis Route 1-14 better addresses intervenor concerns regarding Community and Historic

Values.26 Whitis Route 1-14:

       a. avoids Link F34 and Florence Elementary School;27

       b. crosses only one cultural-resource site,28 compared the PFD’s Focus Routes, which all
          cross at least two;29

       c. crosses only 44.62 miles of areas with high potential for archeological or historical
          sites, fewer than any Focus Route in the PFD;30

       d. contains only 147.64 miles of rangeland pasture, outperforming all Focus Routes in the
          PFD by at least six miles;31

       e. affects only 10.7 miles of cropland/hay meadow, fewer than all Focus Routes contained
          in the PFD;32 and

       f. crosses no upland woodlands.33

       These factors continue to add relevance to cost differences discussed herein. Should the

Commission choose to approve a route in this docket, it should consider the weight that

Community and Historic Values add to Whitis Route 1-14’s overall performance.

                                            III.     CONCLUSION

        Whitis supports the ALJs’ conclusion that Applicants failed to make an independent

showing of need for this line. Whitis therefore requests that the Commission follow the PFD’s

recommendation and deny Applicants’ applications for Import Path 2.

        Should the Commission decline to follow the ALJs’ recommendation and proceed to route

selection, Whitis requests that the Commission sustain these exceptions; select Whitis Route 1-14

or another route that avoids Link F1; modify the PFD accordingly, including modifications

requiring Applicants’ cooperation with landowners to avoid bisection of properties, and grant

Whitis all other relief to which it is entitled.
